claims.text: The subject material is a multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy containing distinct coexisting phases with different mechanical responses.
Mechanical wear preferentially plastically deforms the softer eutectic-phase regions.
Wear-induced plastic deformation produces an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer.
The near-surface transformation proceeds through dynamic recrystallization or amorphization.
The ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior.
The ultra-nanocrystalline layer has a high density of grain boundaries.
The high density of grain boundaries makes the transformed layer more chemically reactive toward the corrosive medium.
Enhanced chemical reactivity of the transformed layer accelerates corrosion during concurrent wear.
Formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer can be associated with low friction and high wear resistance.
The alloy's initial wear resistance may remain relatively high under coupled wear-corrosion conditions.
Concurrent wear and corrosion will produce a higher corrosion rate than the proposed baseline.
Concurrent wear and corrosion will significantly increase total material degradation relative to the proposed baseline.
The proposed coupled-degradation mechanism requires simultaneous aggressive wear, a corrosive environment, and elevated temperature.
The mechanism may not operate under inert conditions, at lower temperatures, or in single-phase HEAs with stable microstructures.
A controlled comparison can expose one specimen set to simultaneous wear and corrosion and another to wear alone at the same elevated temperature and mechanical conditions.
Grain size, nanostructure, wear rate, corrosion rate, total degradation, and surface chemistry can be measured to test the hypothesis.
Failure of the coupled-condition specimens to form significantly more ultra-nanocrystalline material than the wear-only specimens would falsify the proposed mechanism.
Failure of the corrosion rate under coupled conditions to exceed that of the wear-only control would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The mechanism attributes formation of the ultra-nanocrystalline layer primarily to mechanical wear and plastic deformation, so identical wear conditions could produce the layer in both groups. Requiring significantly more of the layer under coupled corrosion is therefore not a necessary prediction of the stated mechanism.

The experimental control has no corrosive medium, yet the falsification rule compares its corrosion rate with that under coupled exposure. A wear-only specimen does not provide a meaningful matched corrosion response; a corrosion-only or otherwise electrochemically matched control would be needed.
